title: Ocular Candidiasis: The Clinical Compendium
summary: Ocular candidiasis is a sight-threatening intraocular infection, typically arising from hematogenous dissemination. This guide provides a deep-dive into the pathophysiology, diagnostic 'string-of-pearls' findings, and the latest evidence-based management protocols for residents and vitreoretinal fellows.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: Ocular candidiasis refers to intraocular infection caused by Candida species. It presents in two primary forms: Candida Chorioretinitis (infection confined to the retina and choroid) and Candida Endophthalmitis (infection involving the vitreous humor). It is most commonly a manifestation of disseminated candidemia, often requiring a multidisciplinary approach involving ophthalmology, infectious disease, and internal medicine.

sections.title: Pathophysiology Flow
content: Step 1: Primary infection or colonization (Gut, Skin, or IV site).
Step 2: Breakdown of mucosal barriers leads to Candidemia.
Step 3: Hematogenous seeding of the highly vascularized Choroid.
Step 4: Breakthrough of the Blood-Retinal Barrier into the Subretinal space.
Step 5: Invasion of the Neurosensory Retina.
Step 6: Vitreous seeding and inflammatory cascade (Endophthalmitis).

rows: Significant blur, floaters, and decreased vision.

sections.title: Comprehensive Ocular Findings
content: Early: Small, round, creamy-white 'fluffy' chorioretinal lesions (<1mm).
Evolution: Lesions enlarge and extend into the vitreous.
Vitreous: 'Cotton ball' opacities or 'string of pearls' (pseudohyphae colonies).
Anterior Segment: Mild cell/flare; occasionally large hypopyon in severe cases.
Vascular: Perivasculitis and retinal hemorrhages (Roth spots).
Late Stage: Tractional retinal detachment or epiretinal membrane formation.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: 1. Dilated Fundus Exam: Gold standard for screening.
2. Blood Cultures: Minimum 2 sets (yield is only 50-60% in chronic cases).
3. Vitreous Tap/Biopsy: For culture, Gram/GMS stain, and PCR (Higher yield than aqueous).
4. OCT: Identify depth of lesions and monitoring subretinal fluid.
5. B-Scan Ultrasound: If media is opaque to rule out RD and assess vitreous membranes.
6. Systemic Search: Echocardiogram (Vegetations) and Renal US (Abscesses).

sections.title: Intravitreal Pharmacotherapy
content: Indication: Mandatory for all cases with vitreous involvement (Endophthalmitis).
Amphotericin B Deoxycholate: 5-10 µg in 0.1 mL (Note: Highly toxic to retina if dose exceeds this).
Voriconazole: 100 µg in 0.1 mL (Safe and well-tolerated).
Frequency: May repeat every 48-72 hours based on clinical response.

sections.title: Surgical Intervention: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV)
content: 1. Indication: Significant vitreous opacification or failure of medical therapy.
2. Core Vitrectomy: Removal of fungal load and inflammatory debris.
3. Targeted Sampling: Obtain undiluted vitreous for microbiology.
4. Induction of PVD: Careful management as hyaloid is often very adherent.
5. Intraoperative Intravitreal: Inject antifungal at the end of the case.

sections.title: Red Flags: Emergency Signs
content: Rapidly progressive vision loss despite systemic fluconazole.
Macular involving chorioretinal lesions (Threatens central vision).
Development of 'String of Pearls' in a patient previously on systemic meds only.
Signs of orbital cellulitis (Suspect Mucor or aggressive Aspergillus in immunocompromised).
Painful eye in the setting of fungemia (Suggests panophthalmitis).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Duration of treatment: Minimum 4-6 weeks total; continue for 2 weeks after resolution of lesions.
Screening Guidelines: AAO now suggests screening ONLY if patient has symptoms or is unable to communicate.
Resistance: Candida glabrata and krusei are often resistant to azoles; use Voriconazole or Ampho B.
The 'Lawn-Mower' Effect: Lesions heal from the periphery inward, leaving behind atrophic scars.

content.explanation: P: Peripheral fluffy lesions; E: Exudates in Vitreous; A: Aqueous cell/flare; R: Retinal involvement (Deep); L: Long-term IV access (Risk); S: String of pearls appearance.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Evidence
sections.content: Recent IDSA and AAO statements emphasize that the incidence of ocular involvement in candidemia has dropped significantly (~1-2%) due to earlier initiation of systemic therapy. This has led to a shift away from mandatory universal screening of all candidemic patients, focusing instead on those with visual symptoms or high-risk systemic factors (e.g., persistent candidemia despite treatment).

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Prognosis: Generally good for C. albicans if caught early.
Tractional Retinal Detachment: Secondary to vitreous membranes.
Epiretinal Membrane: Very common sequela of macular lesions.
Cataract: Due to inflammation or prolonged steroid use post-op.
Phthisis Bulbi: Rare, but possible in end-stage/untreated cases.
